desc:
You are given a sequence path of values and a binary tree tree. Decide whether the tree contains a downward path whose node values, read from top to bottom, are exactly path. A downward path starts at any node, moves from a node to one of its children at every step, and may stop at any node (it does not have to end at a leaf).

Return true if such a path exists and false otherwise. The empty tree contains no path.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

The tree uses this encoding; path is an ordinary array of values. For tree = [5, 2, 4, 1, 6, 3] (root 5 with children 2 and 4; node 2 has children 1 and 6; node 4 has left child 3): path = [2, 6] gives true, path = [5, 4, 3] gives true, and path = [2, 4] gives false because 4 is not a child of 2.
constraints: The tree array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: Try every node as the start of the path and walk down comparing with the sequence. That is correct; the question is how slow it gets when values repeat a lot.
A downward path is a substring of some root-to-node path. So you can search for path as a pattern while walking down from the root, carrying the length of the longest suffix matched so far.

Precompute the KMP failure table of path. During a depth-first walk keep the match length for each node (it is derived from its parent's match length), and answer true as soon as some node reaches a match length equal to path.length.
editorial: The brute force starts a fresh comparison at every node and recurses into both children while the values keep matching. It is correct, but with many equal values (a long chain of zeros against a long list of zeros) it can compare close to n · m pairs, which is acceptable at these limits but is the starting point for something better.

Every downward path is a contiguous piece of a root-to-node path, so the task is string matching along the tree. Compute the KMP failure function of path. Walk the tree from the root; for each node derive its match length from its parent's match length by the usual KMP step (follow failure links while the next expected value differs, then extend by one when it matches). Different children of a node both start from the parent's state, which is why the state is stored per node (or passed down in the DFS stack) instead of in one global variable.

If any node reaches match length m = path.length, the path exists. Each node does a number of failure hops bounded by its current match length, so the total is O(n + m) for typical inputs and never worse than O(n · m); memory is O(n + m).
